newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - IFCT steps up with FRN.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - IFCT steps up with FRN.

text.p: Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand stepped into the Asian debt markets with a step-up floating rate note issue on Monday.
The issue, initially conceived as a straight five-year note, was rejigged to include a put after three years and a step-up coupon.
The US$150 million note issue was launched at par to float at 30 basis points over the six-month London Interbank Offered Rate for the first three years and 37 basis points over LIBOR thereafter.
Fees are 21 basis points flat to give an all-in return of 37 basis points to the put. If held for five years, the issue would pay about 41.2 basis points.
BA Asia and Nomura International (Hong Kong) are joint leads and bookrunners.
The structure of the deal reportedly was changed because investors showed more interest in three-year paper than in five-year paper.
The notes were issued off the borrower's US$3.0 billion global medium-term note programme.
Comment on the issue's pricing ranged from "too tight" to "just about right."
IFCT reportedly has an FRN due in 2002 trading in the secondary market at around 43 basis points over LIBOR.
A few other Thai banks also are looking for dollar funding at similar pricing, bankers said.
They said Farmers Bank is eyeing five-year paper for about 42.5 basis points all-in, while Krung Thai bank is seen paying 40-45 basis points for the same tenor.
Bankers said that while investors have started to buy Thai credits selectively, the mood remains cautious.
"There is some buying interest at the margin, with some investors bottom fishing," said a syndicate manager at a U.S. bank. But he said buying has not been aggressive.
A manager at a European bank agreed.
"The overall sentiment about Thailand has not yet recovered," the banker said.
"There are several Thai deals in the pipeline, and with a very strong credit there is still some appetite. But a lot of investors have withdrawn from the market," he added.
Siam Commercial Bank and Bank of Ayudhya reportedly are looking to the U.S. Yankee market to issue long-term subordinated debt.
In other news, Philippines company C&P Homes launches a US$150 million floating rate note through joint lead managers CS First Boston and ING Barings.
The five-and-one-half-year notes were launched at par and re-offered at 99.80 to float at 212.5 basis points over six-month LIBOR. The all-in return for top-tier participants is 221.6 basis points.
In London, Toyota Motor Credit Corp, a unit of Toyota Motor Corp, launched a US$1.0 billion Euro-Asian bond. CS First Boston and Merrill Lynch International are joint lead managers.
Looking ahead, China confirmed speculation that it would issue a mark-denominated Eurobond.
The official Xinhua news agency said the issue would be made by the Ministry of Finance on behalf of the government. The size and tenor of the deal has not been set.
As expected, CS First Boston and Deutsche Bank will act as joint lead managers.
Standard Chartered Bank will self-lead a HK$2.0 billion floating rate certificate of deposit issue, bankers said Monday.
Sources said Korean issuers are on the prowl in the Yankee market, even though Korean paper has not performed well lately.
They said Pohang Iron and Steel is contemplating a US$300 million 10-year issue, while the City of Taegu reportedly has taken bids on a US$200 million 10-year bond.
Standard and Poor's Corp assigned a Single-A long-term credit rating to Taegu Municipal City Government last month.
